rows.label: Life satisfaction lost per year in prison or jail (points, 0-10)

source.title: World Database of Happiness, Pappot & Phaff (2004): study NL 2004 (prisoners and controls, the Netherlands)
source.page: general happiness and momentary mood, recoded to 0-10
source.note: Momentary mood, asked three times a day for ten days: prisoners 5.25, controls 6.73. Small non-probability sample (N = 42, 40% non-response). Chason (1975, US, World Database of Happiness) found prisoners at 1.23 on a 1-3 life-satisfaction item against 2.22 for the general population, about half the scale; a systematic review of quality-of-life assessments of offenders (vLex, Law Journals) finds detained offenders below the general population.

rows.explainer: What a year in prison or jail costs a person in life satisfaction, against a year outside. No study found asks prisoners the 0-10 life-satisfaction question beside a comparison group, so happiness and mood stand in for it: 0.77 points of general happiness and 1.48 of momentary mood in the one 0-10 comparison found (42 Dutch prisoners and controls, 2004), about half the scale in an older US survey. US prisons are harsher than Dutch ones, but the controls weren't matched to people who would otherwise be in prison and happiness is not life satisfaction, so the range is wide: 1.2, from 0.5 to 3. Read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted or freedom won (WELLBYs: a point for a year is one).

rows.label: Years of life lost per year in prison (New York State parolees)

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.quote: each additional year in prison produced a 15.6% increase in the odds of death for parolees, which translated to a 2-year decline in life expectancy for each year served in prison

rows.explainer: New York parolees, 1989-2003: 2 years of life expectancy lost per year served. Observational, with longer sentences going to people at higher risk anyway, so the low end is a quarter of it (0.5); high 3. This is mortality, the years a person does not live; the life-satisfaction figure (ls_loss_per_year_incarcerated) is the wellbeing of the years they do live, so a model counting both counts different things. Read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison (years)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Patterson (2013)'s example: about 10 years of life lost for a man of 30 serving 5 years
source.note: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties; the remaining life expectancy is our judgment (40 years, 33 to 47), not a figure from the paper.

rows.explainer: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties, with life expectancy below the general population's: 40 years left (33 to 47). Turns years of life lost into a share of a death.

rows.label: Years from a prison-year until the deaths it causes

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.note: The excess risk is 'highest upon release from prison and declined over time'; the delay is our judgment.

rows.explainer: The excess risk is 'highest upon release from prison and declined over time' (Patterson 2013), recovering over about two thirds of the time served: the rest of the sentence plus a few years after release, 3 years (1 to 8). The deaths come this long after the prison-year, so a model discounts them for the wait.

rows.label: Harm to families and children, as a share of the value of a prison-year averted

source.title: Wakefield and Wildeman (2013), Children of the Prison Boom: Mass Incarceration and the Future of American Inequality, Oxford University Press
source.note: Parental incarceration harms children's wellbeing and behaviour and partners' income; no study puts it on the life-satisfaction or death scale of the prison-year itself, so the share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Partners and children of a person in prison lose income, contact and care: 15% of the value of the prison-year (its life satisfaction and the deaths it causes), from 0 to 40%. Read as a side effect by every model that frees people or keeps them out of prison.

rows.label: Earnings lost after release, as a share of the value of a prison-year averted

source.title: Western (2002), The impact of incarceration on wage mobility and inequality, American Sociological Review 67(4): 526-546
source.note: Prison lowers later wages and wage growth; the life-satisfaction gap of a year inside is measured during the year, so later earnings are outside it. The share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: A year in prison lowers earnings after release (a record, lost work experience), which the life-satisfaction gap measured inside does not cover: 10% of the value of the prison-year, from 0 to 30%. Read as a side effect by every model that frees people or keeps them out of prison.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person freed around 45-50 after a long prison term (years)

source.title: Arias and Xu, United States Life Tables, 2022, National Vital Statistics Reports 74(2), Table 2 (males)
source.page: Table 2 (life table for males), age 50-51; the Human Life-Table Database copy of NVSR 74(2)
source.note: US men of 50 have 29.1 years left in 2022 (49: 29.9); people after long prison terms die younger (Patterson 2013), so ours is lower, a judgment.

rows.explainer: People exonerated after long terms are 45 on average when freed: US men of 50 have 29 years left (2022 life table), people after prison fewer: 26 years, from 21 to 31. Turns years of life lost into a share of a death for people freed at these ages (the 40 years of remaining_life_in_prison is for the younger prison population).
